content: The critical temperature, denoted as Tc, is the temperature above which a material no longer exhibits distinct liquid and gas phases. As the critical temperature is approached, the properties of the gas and liquid phases converge, resulting in a single phase known as a supercritical fluid. Beyond the critical temperature, it is impossible to form a liquid by increasing pressure alone, although sufficient pressure may lead to the formation of a solid. The critical pressure is defined as the vapor pressure of a substance at its critical temperature. On a thermodynamic phase diagram, the point corresponding to the critical temperature and critical pressure is referred to as the critical point of the substance. The critical molar volume is the volume occupied by one mole of a material at its critical temperature and pressure. Critical properties, such as critical temperature, pressure, and molar volume, vary between different materials, much like melting and boiling points. For many pure substances, these critical properties are well-documented in scientific literature. However, determining the critical properties of mixtures is more challenging. Even immiscible liquids, such as oil and water, have a critical temperature and pressure at which the two phases become a single, homogeneous phase. In the context of superconductivity, the critical temperature refers to the temperature below which a material transitions into a superconducting state, characterized by zero electrical resistance. In construction, the critical temperature is the temperature above which structural steel loses its strength and can no longer support loads effectively. This temperature typically ranges between 500°C and 560°C, depending on the country. Ensuring that structural steel components remain below this critical temperature is a key function of passive fire protection systems. From a mathematical perspective, for pure substances, the critical isotherm on a pressure-volume (pV) diagram exhibits an inflection point at the critical point. This relationship can be used to derive parameters for equations of state based on critical properties. The principle of corresponding states suggests that substances at equal reduced pressures and temperatures will also have equal reduced volumes.
